Domazlice
do'mazh-li-tse
n. (Bohemian town on the Bavarian road, German Taus; where the crusading army of 1431 fled without a battle)
Czech Domazlice, from a Slavic personal name Domazl; German Taus is a contraction of the same, the town guarding the Bohemian forest passes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Domazlice guards the road from Bavaria through the Bohemian forest, and in August 1431 it was the point at which the fifth and last crusade against the Hussites ended. A great army of the empire, said to have been the largest yet sent, crossed the frontier under the margrave of Brandenburg with the papal legate Cardinal Cesarini in the camp, and advanced to the town. Prokop the Great came up with the field armies, and the imperial host, hearing the Hussite wagons on the road and the hymn the Hussites sang as they came, broke before contact; the army dissolved, the camp and the guns were abandoned, and the legate escaped with difficulty. No battle was fought. It was the rout at Domazlice which convinced the Council of Basel that the Bohemians had to be negotiated with, and so led to the Judge of Cheb the following year and to the Compacts. The dictionary enters Domazlice for the plainest reason: it is the Reformation's nearest thing to Gideon's battle or to the night the Assyrian camp emptied. A professional army, superior in everything but conviction, heard a hymn and ran. The lesson is not that God will always do so, for he usually does not, but that the issue was never in the numbers.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a rout as the defeat and disorderly flight of an army; a panic as a sudden fright without a visible cause; and a host as an army, a great multitude.

expand to see more

ROUT, n. [Fr. route.] The breaking or defeat of an army or band of troops, or the disorder and confusion of troops thus defeated and put to flight.

PANIC, n. [Gr. from Pan, whose terror was supposed to be sudden.] A sudden fright; particularly, a sudden fright without real cause, or terror inspired by a trifling cause.

HOST, n. [L. hostis.] An army; a number of men embodied for war; any great number or multitude.

LEGATE, n. [L. legatus.] An ambassador; particularly, a cardinal or bishop sent by the pope as his representative.

HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a religious song sung in worship.

Key Scripture

Psa 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

Pro 21:31 — "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD."

Act 16:25 — "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them."

Isa 1:9 — "Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah."

Modern Corruption

Bohemian frontier town where the last crusade against the Hussites broke and fled in August 1431 without a battle being fought.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the triumphalist one. A deliverance like Domazlice is a standing temptation to a church, which concludes from one rout that God is committed to its arms; the Hussites drew that conclusion and were destroyed by their own countrymen at Lipany three years later. The dictionary records the deliverance and refuses the inference. God gave Bohemia a great mercy in 1431 and withdrew it in 1434, and he was not inconsistent in doing so.

The principle to recover is in the psalm: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The dictionary also records the detail the chroniclers preserved, that what the imperial troops heard was singing. A church's psalmody is not a military asset and is not meant to be one; but it is the sound of a people who believe what they are saying, and armies have always been able to tell the difference.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rekeb (H7393), a chariot; Hebrew sarid (H8300), a survivor, a remnant left.

expand to see more

Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, chariotry; “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses”, Psalm 20:7.

Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to call to mind; “we will remember the name of the LORD our God”, Psalm 20:7.

Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, safety; “but safety is of the LORD”, Proverbs 21:31.

Greek humneo (G5214) — to sing a hymn; “Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God”, Acts 16:25.

Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, one left remaining; “had left unto us a very small remnant”, Isaiah 1:9.

Usage

"“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” (Psa 20:7) — the largest crusading host yet sent, broken before contact."

"“but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31) — the camp and the guns abandoned on the Bavarian road, August 1431."

"“Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God” (Act 16:25) — what the imperial troops heard coming up the road."
